To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) leaders' role expectations of achieving group goals lead to an increased appraisal of goal importance and (2) this increased appraisal of group goal importance, in turn, increases the moral permissibility to engage in questionable behavior to achieve those goals.
leaders are more likely to make unethical decisions than followers because they are expected to achieve group goals, which is consistent with their role expectations.
the social role of leader contributes to an over valuing of the group goals and a greater moral permissiveness of the means used by leaders to achieve these group goals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social roles people occupy and the expectations that are associated with them and their impact on unethical behavior.
the social role expectations associated with the leader role and their impact on the ethical decision making and behavior of leaders.
the social role expectations and the role of group goals in the ethical decision making and behavior of leaders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role expectations of leaders, relative to group members, contribute to the increased moral permissibility and unethical decision making to achieve group goals.
the social role of leader is associated with a greater valuation of the goals and greater moral justification of the means used for achieving the goals.
leaders' social role expectations contribute to unethical leadership by encouraging the over valuing and pursuit of group goals and by increasing the permissibility of means to achieve group goals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social role of leader is associated with a greater moral license for the means of goal achievement.
leaders' role expectations contribute to the moral failures of leadership by increasing the importance of group goals and the permissibility of unethical means to achieve these goals.

leaders, relative to group members, are more likely to justify morally questionable behavior in order to achieve group goals and that these effects are driven by the social role expectations associated with leadership and the goal importance of the group.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the social roles of leader and group member have important implications for the moral behavior of leaders.

the social role of leader, in contrast to the psychological effects of leader power, contributes to the overvaluing of group goals which, in turn, increases the moral permissibility for leaders to engage in unethical behavior.
